description:
fetch_session (client.rs:279), call (client.rs:333), and upload_blob (blob.rs:262) all call resp.bytes().await which buffers the entire response body into memory BEFORE checking the size cap. The Content-Length pre-check at lines 274/328/254 fires only when the server actually sends Content-Length AND it exceeds the limit. A hostile or compromised server that sends chunked Transfer-Encoding without Content-Length, or that under-reports Content-Length, forces the client to allocate up to whatever the server actually sends before the per-byte check fires.

Trigger: server sends 1 GiB body with chunked encoding and no Content-Length, against a fetch_session call whose limit is 1 MiB.
Behavior: client allocates ~1 GiB in resp.bytes().await, then the post-buffer check at client.rs:280 returns ResponseTooLarge. Memory is reclaimed after the check, but the peak allocation already occurred — sufficient to OOM-kill the client on low-memory devices.

This is precisely the pattern the author got RIGHT in download_blob (blob.rs:372-385): bytes_stream() + per-chunk accumulation + per-chunk cap check. The comment at blob.rs:368-371 explicitly says 'This prevents buffering a response that exceeds the limit when Content-Length is absent or lying — without this, resp.bytes().await would buffer the full response before the check could fire.' The same comment justifies treating the other three paths the same way.

Threat model: matters when connecting to untrusted servers (federation peers, third-party JMAP services, DNS-hijacked endpoints, MITM scenarios). Less acute against Fastmail-style trusted servers, but defense-in-depth.

Fix: replicate download_blob's bytes_stream() pattern in fetch_session, call, and upload_blob. The Content-Length pre-check is still useful as a fast-path rejection for honest oversized responses but cannot be relied on as the only guard.
title: fetch_session/call/upload_blob buffer entire body before size cap check (DOS vs hostile server)
